opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the most immediate thing is that they're changing the interface. For decades, if you wanted a robot to do something, you had to program it, or at least specify things in very precise, structured terms: coordinates, waypoints, object models. What vision language models allow is for a person to just say, in ordinary language, "Could you clear the dishes off the table?" or "Hand me the red mug next to the laptop," and the system can connect those words to what it's actually seeing in the camera image. That's a real shift. It makes robots far more accessible to people who aren't engineers.

They also bring something we've struggled with for a long time, which is a kind of common sense about the world. A VLM has absorbed an enormous amount of knowledge from text and images, so it knows that a mug usually has a handle, that you don't put a knife in a drawer blade-up, that a towel is soft and deformable. That kind of semantic, high-level knowledge is very helpful for task planning, for breaking "tidy up the kitchen" into a sequence of sensible steps.

But I want to be careful here, because I think there's a tendency to overstate what this solves. Knowing *what* to do is different from knowing *how* to do it physically. The VLM can tell you to pick up the mug, but actually grasping it reliably, with the right forces, dealing with friction, slight errors in perception, an object that's partially occluded or slippery, that's still extremely hard. I often talk about this as the gap between the language world and the physical world. Language models were trained on vast amounts of internet data; there's no comparable internet-scale dataset of robot interactions. So there's a data gap, and I think it'll take quite a while to close.

So where I see the real promise right now is in combining these approaches: using vision language models for the high-level understanding and communication with humans, and pairing them with good old-fashioned engineering, physics, geometry, control theory, for the low-level manipulation. Just as importantly, they could make robots better at explaining themselves and asking for help. A robot that can say "I'm not sure which of these two cups you mean," or "I tried to grasp this and it slipped, should I try again?" That kind of two-way interaction, where humans and robots collaborate, is what I'm most excited about, more than the idea of fully autonomous robots that do everything on their own.

r001.rationale: The response says a robot can connect a natural-language description such as “the red mug next to the laptop” to what it sees in the camera image.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe NeRFs or constructing a scene model from images for rendering unseen viewpoints.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the most immediate thing is that we can finally talk to robots. For most of my career, if you wanted a robot to do something, you had to program it very explicitly, or set up some elaborate teleoperation rig. Now you can say, "Pick up the red mug and put it in the sink," and the vision language model can look at the scene, figure out what the red mug is, understand what a sink is, and parse the intent. That's a big deal. Natural language is the interface humans have been using with each other for a very long time, and now it works, at least at that semantic level, with machines.

The other thing I find exciting is common sense. These models have absorbed an enormous amount about how the world works: that a glass of water will spill if you tip it, that you shouldn't put a laptop in the dishwasher, that a knife has a sharp side. Robots historically had none of that. They were brilliant at repeating a motion a million times in a factory and hopeless the moment anything deviated. So having this huge reservoir of world knowledge available is going to make robots much more flexible in unstructured settings like homes and hospitals.

But I always like to add a caveat here, because I think there's a lot of hype. The language and perception side has moved very fast. The physical side, actually grasping, manipulating, doing something dexterous with your hands, has not moved at the same pace. I sometimes call this the "data gap." Language models trained on something like the entire internet, trillions of tokens. Robots don't have anything like that. Every bit of real-world manipulation data has to be collected physically, one trial at a time, and it's slow and expensive and messy.

So where I see vision language models really helping in the near term is at the high level: understanding the task, decomposing it into steps, deciding what to do next, recovering when something goes wrong. And then underneath that, you still need good control, good grasp planning, good physics. I think the winning approach is going to combine these, what I've been calling good old-fashioned engineering together with learning. The model tells you what to do, and well-understood robotics tells you how to actually do it without knocking the mug off the counter.

r001.rationale: The response says the model can look at the scene, identify which object is the red mug, and connect that visual object to the spoken instruction.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention NeRFs or constructing a scene model that can render unseen viewpoints.

astra-6.text:
What’s exciting to me is that they could let us communicate with robots at a much higher level. Instead of specifying every motion, you could say, “Can you help me clean up this table?” The robot could use what it sees, together with your request, to work out which objects you’re referring to and what needs to happen.

And it could be a dialogue. If you say, “Bring me that cup,” and there are three cups, the robot could ask, “Do you mean the blue one?” That ability to connect language to the scene, and then ask for clarification, could make robots much easier to work with.

The challenge is that understanding a request isn’t the same as being able to carry it out. You still have to grasp the cup, account for what’s inside it, and move it without spilling. So I see these models as a very promising interface, but we still need reliable ways to connect their interpretations to physical actions—and to recognize when the robot should stop and ask for help.

r001.rationale: The response says the robot can combine what it sees with a language request to identify which objects are being referred to, including clarifying which cup when several are present.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention NeRFs or constructing a scene model from images for rendering unseen viewpoints.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting possibility is that you could talk to a robot in ordinary language, and it could connect what you’re saying to what it sees. You could say, “Could you clear the table?” rather than having to specify every object and every motion. And if something is ambiguous, it could ask you a question: “Do you want me to put this away, or leave it here?”

That could make robots much easier to work with. But there’s still a gap between recognizing an object, talking sensibly about it, and actually manipulating it. A model might give a very plausible description of how to pick up a glass, but that doesn’t mean the robot can reliably do it. It has to deal with geometry, contact, friction—all the details of the physical world.

So I’m excited about these models as an interface, and as a way of bringing more context into planning. The challenge is connecting that to actions that are reliable, and having the robot recognize when it needs help.

r001.rationale: The response says the robot could connect what a person says to what it sees, with the table-clearing example; this communicates grounding language in the visual scene.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention NeRFs, scene reconstruction from images, or rendering from unseen viewpoints.
